items.title: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress
items.summary: Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0 extends previous benchmarks to measure an agent's ability to sustain progress over extended workflows using process rewards. It incorporates 77 tasks across 13 domains and eight task types, created through a systematic reconstruction pipeline. The evaluation horizon is increased to three hours, allowing for measurement of sustained progress via recorded checkpoints. Experiments showed GPT-6-astra led with a dense mean reward of 0.69 across 37 tasks at a threshold of 0.95. The work provides a more process-aware testbed for assessing reliable agent execution over long durations.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress" details an extension of benchmarks designed to assess an agent's ability to sustain progress over extended workflows using process rewards. The research introduced Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0, which incorporates seventy-seven tasks across thirteen domains and eight task types generated via a systematic reconstruction pipeline. Evaluation of agent performance extended to a three-hour horizon, enabling the measurement of sustained progress through recorded checkpoints. Experiments demonstrated that the GPT-6-astra model achieved a dense mean reward of zero point six nine across thirty-seven tasks when evaluated against a threshold of zero point nine five. This work establishes a more process-aware testbed for assessing reliable agent execution over extended durations. Future developments in agent evaluation will likely focus on long-term performance metrics.

items.title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
items.summary: The paper proposes a C-test for supraintelligence based on Levin's Kt, which relates difficulty to the complexity of the underlying mechanism. It uses Large Language Models (LLMs) as representational machines to conduct this test. The research formalizes a measure and develops a pipeline to certify test items based on this framework. A battery of certified items was administered to twelve LLMs, showing agent characteristics decreasing with difficulty. This work explores the limits of certification for supra-intelligence beyond current frontier models.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence" details a method for assessing supraintelligence using Large Language Models as representational machines. The research proposes a C-test based on Levin's Kt to measure difficulty relative to underlying mechanism complexity, and a pipeline for certifying test items. A battery of certified items was administered to twelve Large Language Models, demonstrating that agent characteristics exhibited a decrease as the difficulty level increased. This work investigates the limits of certification for supra-intelligence beyond current frontier models. The findings establish a framework for empirically testing and certifying advanced intelligence capabilities in artificial systems. Further research will explore the scalability of this certification method for future AI developments.

items.title: Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs
items.summary: Cloud-hosted models provide the most accurate agent performance by accessing private user data. Local models running on edge devices keep data private but perform poorly without external context. An intermediate architecture proposes having cloud models delegate bounded data questions to small local models via function calls. This approach improves code-only agent success rates by up to 14.9 percentage points compared to cloud-hosted methods. This research explores using local models as interpreters in cloud-written agent programs.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Should SLMs be in the Driver's Seat? A Study of Local Models as Interpreters in Cloud-Written Agent Programs" details an investigation into utilizing local models as interpreters within cloud-written agent programs. This research demonstrates that an intermediate architecture employing cloud models to delegate bounded data questions to small local models via function calls improves code-only agent success rates by up to fourteen point nine percentage points compared to purely cloud-hosted methods. The study explored the performance dynamics between cloud-hosted models, which access private user data for high accuracy, and local models, which ensure data privacy on edge devices. The proposed intermediate architecture successfully balanced data access and local computation, showing a tangible increase in agent performance by leveraging local model interpretation. This work indicates a viable pathway for integrating privacy-preserving local models into complex, cloud-managed agent systems.

items.title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
items.summary: Evaluations of agentic data science often focus only on downstream performance and code correctness, overlooking fundamental data science principles. The research argues that these assessments fail to capture methodological failures like data leakage and inappropriate validation. The authors conducted a multi-faceted evaluation across 220 tasks, a custom test suite, and qualitative analysis against expert solutions. Findings indicate that most agentic solutions contain failures, and data leakage correlates with poor predictive performance. Ultimately, principled failure mode analysis should be integrated into agentic data science evaluations for building trustworthy systems.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science" details an evaluation that reveals systemic failures in assessing agentic data science based solely on downstream performance and code correctness. The research involved a multi-faceted evaluation across two hundred twenty tasks and a custom test suite, alongside qualitative analysis against expert solutions. Findings demonstrated that most agentic solutions exhibited failures, and a direct correlation was established between data leakage and poor predictive performance. The study concludes that principled failure mode analysis must be integrated into agentic data science evaluations to foster trustworthy systems. This necessitates a shift in evaluation practices for building reliable artificial intelligence systems.

items.title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function
items.summary: Counterfactual interventions were applied to a Proximal Policy Optimization agent's value function to explore if it functions as a world model in the Crafter environment. Despite optimizing only for reward, the value function learned environmental concepts such as collectible rules, health impacts of resources, and inventory heuristics. This suggests that model-free reinforcement learning may implicitly learn environmental representations. The study also discusses the safety implications of these visualizations and current limitations in agent intelligence. Ultimately, it raises questions about what constitutes a truly learned world model in reinforcement learning.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function" explores the potential for reinforcement learning agents to implicitly develop world models through value function analysis. The study found that counterfactual interventions applied to a Proximal Policy Optimization agent's value function, even when optimizing solely for reward, resulted in the learning of environmental concepts such as collectible rules, resource health impacts, and inventory heuristics. The research details the application of counterfactual interventions within the Crafter environment to probe the value function's structure. The methodology demonstrated that the learned value function encoded these environmental representations, suggesting that model-free reinforcement learning may implicitly acquire environmental understanding. The investigation also addresses the safety considerations and current limitations regarding agent intelligence in this context. Future research must define the criteria for a truly learned world model in reinforcement learning systems.

items.title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data
items.summary: Inverse reasoning models use answer-only data to generate reasoning traces, treating the Chain-of-Thought as latent variables. A partner inverse reasoning LLM is trained to generate these traces conditioned on the answers, allowing the inverse model to be reused efficiently. This approach facilitates post-training and verification from answer-only data, addressing the inefficiency of requiring full reasoning traces. Distillation from this inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 performance on hard prompts compared to self-distillation methods. The inverse model also functions as an accurate verifier, improving selection accuracy in evaluation tasks.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data" reports on inverse reasoning models that utilize answer-only data to generate reasoning traces, achieving efficiency in post-training and verification processes. The research details the training of a partner inverse reasoning large language model to generate reasoning traces conditioned solely on the provided answers, treating the Chain-of-Thought as latent variables. This methodology allows the inverse model to be reused efficiently, addressing the inefficiency of requiring full reasoning traces. Distillation from this inverse model demonstrated that performance at one pass compared to hard prompts is roughly doubled when compared to self-distillation methods. Furthermore, the inverse model functions as an accurate verifier, enhancing selection accuracy in evaluation tasks. This work suggests a pathway for more efficient and verifiable large language model training and evaluation.

items.title: PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization
items.summary: PMO-Dock introduces a benchmark and protocol for docking-based molecular optimization, addressing the lack of standardization in the field. It includes 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task that penalizes off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development and final evaluation, using held-out test tasks for final assessment under a strict oracle budget. Four diverse methods, including Saturn, GenMol, Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama, are benchmarked against this protocol. Results indicate that no single method is universally superior, suggesting method-dependent selection strategies based on generalization and sample efficiency.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "PMO-Dock: Benchmarking Docking, Specificity, and Generalization in Molecular Optimization" introduces a benchmark and protocol for docking-based molecular optimization that addresses the lack of standardization in the field. The protocol encompasses twenty-five tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task designed to penalize off-target interactions, separating model development from final evaluation using held-out test tasks under a strict oracle budget. Four diverse methods, including Saturn, GenMol, Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama, were benchmarked against this protocol, revealing that no single method demonstrates universal superiority, suggesting that method-dependent selection strategies based on generalization and sample efficiency are necessary. This research establishes a standardized framework for evaluating molecular optimization algorithms in computational chemistry.

items.title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
items.summary: The study investigates how the repetition of samples affects performance in image self-distillation models, challenging the assumption that more unique samples always yield better results. Experiments across various datasets revealed that the effect of sample repetition is dataset-dependent and non-trivial. The authors propose a modified Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly incorporates both the number of unique samples and repetition per sample. This new formulation aims to better capture the data-compute trade-offs in these distillation tasks. The research also explores the impact of subset selection and augmentation on downstream performance.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation" investigates how the repetition of samples affects performance in image self-distillation models, revealing that this effect is dataset-dependent and non-trivial. Experiments across various datasets demonstrated that the assumption of more unique samples always yielding better results is challenged by the presence of sample repetition. Researchers explored the impact of sample repetition and subset selection on downstream performance, proposing a modified Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly incorporates both the number of unique samples and the repetition per sample to better capture data-compute trade-offs in these distillation tasks. This research also examined the influence of augmentation on the final outcomes. The findings suggest that distillation model scaling must account for sample redundancy to accurately predict performance gains.

items.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
items.summary: ClawLoop is a framework designed to enable self-improving agents within harness environments without relying on external teacher models. It operates through a self-sustaining cycle involving Task Synthesis, Training, and Diagnosis and Feedback phases. Task Synthesis generates training tasks, while Diagnosis analyzes agent behavior to produce feedback for subsequent task generation. The process involves updating the agent via Supervised Fine-Tuning or Reinforcement Learning. Using Qwen3.6-27B, ClawLoop achieved consistent improvements on several benchmarks, with gains also observed when transferring refined tasks to smaller models.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop" details a framework for self-improving agents operating within harness environments without external teacher models, demonstrating consistent performance gains through an internal training loop. The framework operates through a self-sustaining cycle involving Task Synthesis, Training, and Diagnosis and Feedback phases, where task synthesis generates training tasks, diagnosis analyzes agent behavior to produce feedback for subsequent task generation, and agent updates are performed via supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. Utilizing the Qwen3.6-27B model, ClawLoop achieved consistent improvements across several benchmarks, and gains were also observed when transferring refined tasks to smaller models. This development suggests a pathway toward autonomous agent development through endogenous learning mechanisms.

items.title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
items.summary: The work introduces MOSAIC, a method to attribute training-example influence in vision-language models by learning a shared, sparse image-text latent space. MOSAIC encodes this space with properties ensuring sparsity, contiguity, alignment to descriptive phrases, and decorrelation. It then uses EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence, localizing contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. Evaluation on models like Qwen and Gemma shows that these learned features are more localized and coherent. The research demonstrates that visual evidence substantially reorganizes training-data attribution while preserving shared latent structure.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models" introduces a method for attributing training-example influence in vision-language models by learning a shared, sparse image-text latent space. The research details the development of MOSAIC, a method that encodes this shared latent space with properties including sparsity, contiguity, alignment to descriptive phrases, and decorrelation. This framework then employs EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence, allowing for the localization of contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. Evaluation on models such as Qwen and Gemma indicates that the learned features exhibit greater localization and coherence, demonstrating that visual evidence significantly reorganizes training-data attribution while maintaining shared latent structure. This work suggests new avenues for understanding and manipulating the internal representations of multimodal models.

items.title: Correction Training for Diffusion Models
items.summary: Iterative sampling in diffusion models causes error accumulation due to exposure bias between training and inference. A correction step is introduced to reduce this training-inference gap by training a corrector against the base model's predictions. During sampling, this corrector iteratively refines the denoiser's clean-sample predictions at intermediate denoising steps. This approach substantially improves sample quality without losing diversity and achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance. The method shows that the increased inference cost can be managed by distilling refined predictions back into the base model.

items.title: VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
items.summary: VETNET is an ecosystem of benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks for advancing AI in animal science and veterinary medicine. It aims to standardize high-quality datasets through multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework seeks to bridge the gap between AI progress in human medicine and the fragmented development of veterinary AI. The project focuses on assembling standardized data to drive innovation in the veterinary field.

items.title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
items.summary: The study compares open-weight and closed frontier language models for security tasks using the CTI-REALM benchmark. The research finds that an open-weight model can achieve results comparable to the strongest closed models at less than one-tenth of the cost, given sufficient interaction turns. The benchmark's message limit acts as a confound, and results are more robust when the limit is relaxed. Stage-level metrics are proposed to better assess agent performance by evaluating submitted outputs against the ground truth. This suggests routing workflow stages to the best-performing model rather than relying on a single overall score.

items.title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
items.summary: The research introduces forecast grounding as a pretraining principle for time-series language models, ensuring learned representations retain predictive temporal information. The LOTUS method instantiates this by predicting the next patch from LLM hidden states to encourage temporal awareness. A temporal-spectral patch representation is also proposed to capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns. LOTUS achieved 59.91% accuracy across multiple evaluations, outperforming baselines significantly with minimal trainable parameters. These results confirm that forecast grounding effectively enables compact time-series language models to excel.

items.title: Neural Supervised Clustering for Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments
items.summary: The research proposes nonlinear supervised clustering fusion (NSCF) to learn individualized treatment rules from many treatments. This framework uses a neural Q-learning approach with shared nonlinear covariate representation and low-dimensional treatment embeddings. It groups treatments with similar learned contrasts to yield an individualized treatment rule and an interpretable partition. An alternating algorithm combines neural training, embedding fusion, partition selection, and grouped refitting. Results show that NSCF improves policy value in a melanoma xenograft application, supporting nonlinear representation learning with supervised treatment fusion.

items.title: Bayesian Causal Forests for Zero-Inflated Continuous Outcomes
items.summary: Estimating treatment effects is difficult when outcomes exhibit a discrete zero mass and a skewed continuous distribution. The proposed method, ZIC-BCF-Smear, is a decoupled, two-part nonparametric estimator for zero-inflated continuous outcomes. It models participation with a Probit BCF and positive intensity with a Gaussian BCF, using Propensity Adjustment and Duan's smearing for re-transformation. Simulations confirm this method matches well-specified models without their assumptions. The technique was applied to estimate effects in a cancer trial concerning severe toxicity.

items.title: Conformalized Physics-Informed Weak Regression for Parameter Estimation in Epidemic Models
items.summary: The research introduces physics-informed weak regression (PIWR) for parameter estimation in epidemic models, aiming to provide distribution-free uncertainty. PIWR integrates the model over time, estimates the initial state jointly, and requires no data derivatives. This method, combined with split conformal prediction, yields simultaneous parameter intervals with finite-sample coverage guarantees. Experiments show PIWR and related methods are significantly more accurate than standard physics-informed methods and DINNs. The approach facilitates fast estimation while ensuring reliable uncertainty quantification for disease models.

items.title: IR-PRM+ with Previous-Utility Prediction: Constant Regret and Best-Iterate Convergence
items.summary: The work introduces an approach for regret matching in game solving that incorporates previous-utility prediction to achieve stronger theoretical guarantees. This method, IR-PRM+, recovers the constant-regret and convergence-rate guarantees previously seen with extra-gradient prediction for simultaneous and alternating updates. The technique bounds strategy movements and uses the relative growth of the regret-vector norm to prevent unbounded norm growth. These guarantees extend to finite two-player zero-sum matrix games and corresponding extensive-form games under specific conditions. Consequently, the current duality gap vanishes, and the current profile converges to the Nash equilibrium set.

items.title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
items.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies rank-one updates to every token, prompting a question about the necessary number of components per token. The paper introduces SQUELCH, a router-free method that uses soft-thresholding and Stein's unbiased risk estimate to dynamically select active ranks per token. This technique suppresses redundant components by performing an explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix. SQUELCH improves performance over standard LoRA and mixture-of-experts baselines on various reasoning tasks. On commonsense reasoning tasks, SQUELCH activates an average of 8.6 out of 32 components per token.

items.title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
items.summary: Token importance for on-policy distillation is derived from the distillation objective, specifically how much loss can decrease under a local KL budget. This utility is calculated as $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. This method, termed Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), concentrates importance on relevant positions across various distillation criteria. FUW improves performance over uniform distillation for multiple benchmarks and Qwen3 models under both reverse-KL and forward-KL settings. The derived utility is competitive with existing selective methods based on a single objective score.

items.title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
items.summary: The research benchmarks how class-incremental learning (CIL) methods, typically developed for vision, transfer to frozen protein encoders. The study tested nine CIL methods across five different protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets. The results showed that no method reliably transfers across these encoders, indicating instability in the transfer process. This instability stems from weak gradient signals and heterogeneity in embedding geometry, which depend on the dataset scale and encoder. Reliable protein CIL requires encoder-aware methods that adapt to the specific geometry of the representation.

items.title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
items.summary: Machine learning models are used in high-throughput perturbation screens to predict gene effects for untested combinations. Standard out-of-distribution methods often fail when predicting unseen gene interactions, even if individual genes were seen during training. The study introduces "additive disagreement" (AD) to measure the extra interaction effect introduced by the model beyond a simple sum of single-gene effects. Predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Additive disagreement proves to be an informative signal across various compositional settings for agentic perturbation-screening workflows.

items.title: Discrete Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Under Sparsity
items.summary: Discrete diffusion models are investigated for their performance under sparsity assumptions, contrasting with continuous diffusion models. The research analyzes the statistical rates of discrete diffusion models by studying a nonparametric estimator from a regularized score-entropy objective. This analysis establishes minimax-optimal rates for discrete diffusion models in the sparse regime. The proposed regularization method adapts intrinsically to sparsity without needing explicit knowledge of the sparsity parameter, similar to label smoothing. Consequently, discrete diffusion models demonstrate an inherent ability to adapt to sparsity.

items.title: Student Copula Markov Networks
items.summary: The paper extends probabilistic graphical models to non-Gaussian data by characterizing the pairwise Markov property using copula densities. It derives a necessary condition for this property specifically within Student copula Markov networks. An Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm (ECM) is introduced for penalized maximum likelihood estimation and graph selection. Simulation studies evaluate the ECM's effectiveness in estimating parameters and recovering graph structure. The work contributes a new framework for modeling dependencies in these specific network structures.

items.title: Semi-Amortized Bayesian Inference with Reusable Local Posteriors
items.summary: Amortized Bayesian inference is introduced to estimate parameters when likelihoods are computationally expensive or unavailable. The method divides parameters into blocks, leveraging conditional independence to identify necessary information for each block. Neural estimators are trained via simulations to approximate the full conditional posterior for expensive blocks. A Markov chain alternates between draws from these estimators and conventional updates for the remaining variables. This approach allows for the reuse of estimators across different blocks and datasets in complex models.

items.title: Wong--Zakai Convergence and FNO Learning for Stochastic Volterra Equations
items.summary: The paper investigates Wong--Zakai convergence and Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learning for stochastic Volterra integral equations (SVIEs) that model systems with memory. A Wong--Zakai theorem supports the convergence of pathwise solutions when using piecewise linear approximations of Brownian motion. This convergence facilitates the use of mirror-padded Fourier neural operators to learn the solution operator for SVIEs. Numerical experiments show that this method achieves competitive prediction accuracy and generalizes well to finer temporal grids. The study extends prior operator-learning frameworks to SVIEs by analyzing convergence and approximation for convolutional memory.

items.title: Structure-aware Bayesian full waveform inversion via diffusion-regularized Stein variational gradient descent
items.summary: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is improved using Structure-aware Bayesian methods, specifically Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD), to quantify uncertainty. The method incorporates a learned diffusion model as an implicit regularization to capture geological structure, overcoming limitations of simple priors. This combination of FWI data consistency, posterior diversity, and structural realism is achieved. Experiments show that this approach yields more geologically consistent mean models and better uncertainty estimates. Consequently, learned diffusion priors enhance Bayesian FWI stability and interpretability.

items.title: Delay Complexity Dimension: Learning with Delayed and Censored Labels
items.summary: The study investigates the PAC learning of binary classifiers when labels are delivered with random delays and are censored beyond an observation window $W$. It introduces the Delay Complexity Dimension (DCD), which combines the VC dimension with the exact label-information rate of the observation channel. The research shows that learners require $\Omega(\mathrm{DCD}/\varepsilon^2)$ samples, and an oracle pseudo-label ERM achieves this rate. The theory also suggests a quantization scheme where delay information reduces residual label variance, offering an expedition policy guarantee. Experiments indicate that a moderate window can outperform immediate labels, supported by synthetic data and log analysis.

items.title: Generalizing Identifiability Results in Causal Discovery from Complete Data to Missing Data Settings
items.summary: Causal discovery algorithms have been developed for complete data, but methods for handling missing values remain limited. The research establishes general conditions under which causal graphs remain identifiable even with various missingness categories, including Missing Not At Random. Identifiability is preserved if missingness mechanisms do not causally interact, no variable causes its own missingness, and faithfulness or generalized linear models hold for the missingness. Based on these findings, two asymptotically correct algorithms are introduced for Additive Noise Models to recover causal graphs. These results allow for the extension of correctness guarantees from complete data to settings with missing data.

items.title: Scaling Cheap Synthetic Pretraining Improves Indoor Radio-Map Prediction
items.summary: Limited real measurements necessitate using large-scale synthetic pretraining to improve indoor radio-map prediction. The research introduces a pipeline featuring a layout generator and an approximate ray tracer to create diverse synthetic data. Pretraining ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders on 128M synthetic samples, followed by fine-tuning, demonstrated error reduction. The models showed predictable power-law scaling in performance based on data size, even with simulator mismatches. Ultimately, pretraining on cheap simulation data enhances indoor radio-map prediction accuracy when real data is scarce.
